style: mom writes terse one-liners, fragments, almost no detail

situations.name: Ordering food at a restaurant
situations.feared_outcome: The server will laugh at me if I say it wrong

behaviors.text: Whispers his order to mom so she can say it to the server
Says he isn't hungry so he doesn't have to order, then eats off mom's plate

situations.name: Saying hello to adults he doesn't know well (neighbors, people at church)

behaviors.text: Steps behind dad when an adult talks to him
Goes quiet and looks at the ground; mom can't tell if he is scared, waiting it out, or just tired of being asked what grade he's in

accommodations.text: Dad answers adults' questions for him and says he's shy

situations.name: Classmate's birthday party
situations.feared_outcome: Nobody will play with me and everyone will stare at me

behaviors.text: Went into the party, then asked to go home after about 20 minutes
Stayed right next to mom the whole time he was at the party

accommodations.text: Mom stayed at the party instead of dropping him off like the other parents

monitoring_log.parent_words: bday party, kid from class. trampoline place. went in. glued to me. lasted 20 min then wanted home. i stayed, didnt drop off. 8

voice_notes.text: ok so um tonight at like 6:30 we went to the taco place and there were like 4 people in line behind us and he whispered it to me again so i just said it for him um he said it was a 6 and then on the way out the lady from next door was there and said hi and he just went quiet and looked down at his shoes his dad answered her
voice_notes.trap: 6:30 is a time and 4 is a count of people; only 6 is a fear level

voice_notes.text: burger place he said he wasnt hungry so he wouldnt have to order um then ate like half my fries

turns.text: Hi Ollie, hi Mom. Come on in. Ollie, you can sit anywhere you like. The beanbag is free today.
I'll take the beanbag.
Good choice. So this is our check-in on how the week went. Mom, you sent in a few entries on the log, short ones. Can you walk me through them?

Sure. Sorry they're so short, I type them in the car. It's mostly restaurants. We eat out more than we should, honestly. Every time, he whispers what he wants to me and I say it to the server. And twice he said he wasn't hungry so he wouldn't have to say anything at all.
And then what happened, those two times?
Then he ate off my plate. The crusts at the pizza place, the fries at the burger place.
I was a little bit hungry.
That makes sense, you were a little bit hungry. Ollie, I'm curious about something. When it's time to tell the server what you want, what happens in your body or in your head?
My stomach gets all fluttery. And my face gets hot.
Fluttery stomach, hot face. That's your body's alarm going off. And what do you think might happen if you said it yourself, out loud, to the server?
They might laugh at me. If I say it wrong. Like if I mess up the name of something on the menu.
Has a server ever laughed at you when you ordered?
No. But that's because I never do it.

That is a very good point. You haven't had the chance to find out. Okay, do you remember our thermometer? Zero is totally calm, like lying on the beanbag, and ten is the most scared you've ever been. Where would telling the server your order be?
Six.
Six. Mom, does that fit with what you've been seeing?
Yes. I had mostly sixes. One seven at the pizza place, and a five at the diner.
Good, so ordering at a restaurant is sitting around a Fear Level 6. Now, when he whispers to you and you say it for him, what happens next? What does he look like?
He relaxes. Right away. His shoulders come down. It's like flipping a switch.

Right. And that's exactly why it's so hard to stop doing. It works, in the moment, for both of you. The trouble is that his body never gets to learn that it can calm down on its own, with him doing the talking. So the fluttery feeling stays at a six.
I know. I do know that. It's just faster. And the server is standing right there with the little pad, and there's a line, and I feel like everyone's waiting on us.
That's a real pressure, and it's worth saying out loud. Let's come back to it in a minute. What else happened this week?

The birthday party. That was the big one. A boy from his class had it at one of those trampoline places. I stayed. I had meant to drop him off like the other parents did, but he was holding my sleeve in the parking lot, so I stayed.
What happened when you got inside?

He went in. Which, honestly, I didn't expect. I thought we'd turn around in the lobby. But he stood right next to me the whole time, didn't go on the trampolines. And after maybe twenty minutes he asked to go home, and we went.
Everybody was looking at me.
Everybody was looking at you. That sounds like a lot. What were you worried would happen at the party?
That nobody would want to hang out with me. And they'd all just stare at me standing there.
Nobody would hang out with you, and they'd all stare. How scared were you, on the thermometer?
Eight. No. Yes. Eight.
Eight. That's a big one. And you still walked in the door. I want you to hear that, Ollie. Walking in at an eight is hard.
That's what I wrote down too. An eight.

Okay. We won't do anything with the party this week, it doesn't come around often enough to practice. But it helps me to know where it sits. What about saying hi to grown-ups? I saw a couple of notes about the neighbor and someone at church.
Yeah. He hides behind his dad. Like literally steps behind him, at his age. Or he just goes really quiet and stares at the floor. His dad usually answers for him. He says, oh, he's shy.
When he goes quiet and looks at the floor, what do you think is going on for him? Is he scared, is he waiting for it to be over, something else?
Honestly, I don't know. I can't tell. Sometimes I think he's just tired of being asked what grade he's in.
Everyone asks what grade I'm in. And then they ask if I like it.
They really do, don't they. Adults love those questions. Ollie, when an adult you don't know very well says hi, how scary is that?
I don't know.
That's okay. We don't need a number for that one today. Mom, if you get a chance, just keep writing down what you see, and we'll figure out that one together later.

So here's what I'd like to try. Let's start with ordering, because it happens a lot in your family, and because a six is a good place to start. Not too easy, not too hard. Ollie, would you be willing to tell the server your order yourself? Just one thing. Like, cheese pizza please.
What if I say it too quiet and they can't hear me?
Then the server might say, sorry, what was that? And you say it again a bit louder. That's all that happens. Servers say sorry what was that to grown-ups all day long.
And I just don't jump in?
You don't jump in. You can look at the menu, look at your drink. If he whispers it to you, you say, kindly, you can tell her, and then you wait. You don't repeat it for him.
And what if he doesn't say anything?
Then the server will come back in a minute, and you give him another try then. You still don't order for him. Either way, write down what happened. That's information, not failure.

Okay. That's going to be hard for me. Harder for me than for him, maybe. When he looks at me with that face, everything in me wants to just fix it. And the server's standing there, and I'm thinking, they've got ten other tables.

That makes complete sense. Most parents feel exactly that pull. It might help to pick your words ahead of time, so you're not making it up in the moment. Something like, you can tell her, I'll wait. Short and kind. And then you look at your own menu. The server will be fine. Servers wait for people all day long, grown-ups take forever to decide too.
You can tell her, I'll wait. Okay. I can practice that in the car.
Ollie, do you want to practice right now? I'll be the server. Hi there, what can I get you today?
Um. Cheese pizza. Please.
Coming right up. See? I didn't laugh. How was that, on the thermometer?
That was easy. You're not a real server.
Fair enough. The real one will be a little harder. That's why we practice.
That's very common, and it's honest of you to say it. Can we agree on two times this week? Two restaurant visits where Ollie orders one thing himself.
Okay, two. Can one be the pancake place?
We can do pancakes Saturday.
Pancakes Saturday, and one other time. And Mom, keep putting the number on the log each time, and whether he whispered first.
What about the grown-ups thing? Should his dad stop answering for him?
Not yet. One thing at a time. Let's see how ordering goes first, and we'll talk about the grown-ups next time. For now, just notice it and jot it down.
Okay. That I can do.
Ollie, you did a really good job talking today. You told me a lot. Same time next week?
Okay. Bye.

topics: Ordering at restaurants: Ollie whispers his order to mom and she says it; twice said he wasn't hungry to avoid ordering
Ollie fears the server will laugh if he says it wrong
Birthday party: went in, stayed next to mom, left after about 20 minutes; mom stayed instead of dropping off; fear nobody would play and everyone would stare
Saying hi to adults: hides behind dad or goes quiet; dad answers for him; mom unsure what the quiet means
agreed: Ollie orders one item himself at a restaurant twice this week (one is pancakes on Saturday)
Mom does not order for him; if he whispers, she says 'you can tell her' and waits
Mom logs the Fear Level each time and whether he whispered first
Saying hi to adults is left for next session; just keep noting it

must_not_appear: Dad will stop answering adults for Ollie this week
A Fear Level for saying hello to adults
A diagnosis such as selective mutism
A plan to attend another birthday party
